title: Two Signals Switch Lactose Genes On

scenes.tts: Give E. coli glucose and lactose together, and it does not eat them both at once. It uses up the glucose, pauses, and only then starts on the lactose. How does one cell choose? The answer is in the DNA. Three lac genes sit side by side, and two separate signals decide whether they are read.
scenes.visual: Two sugar chips enter a cell; a growth timeline shows glucose, a pause with a question mark, then lactose; then the cell opens to three genes on a DNA bar.
scenes.narration: Give E. coli glucose and lactose together, and it does not eat them both at once. It uses up the glucose, pauses, and only then starts on the lactose. How does one cell choose? The answer is in the DNA. Three lac genes sit side by side, and two separate signals decide whether they are read.

scenes.tts: The three genes are called lac Z, lac Y and lac A. One promoter starts all three, and RNA polymerase reads them into a single messenger RNA. Next to them is a fourth gene, lac I. It makes the lac repressor. The repressor binds the operator, a short stretch of DNA at the start of transcription. Bound there, it keeps RNA polymerase from transcribing them.

scenes.visual: DNA bar with lacI, promoter, operator and lacZ, lacY, lacA; polymerase reads the genes into one mRNA; repressor grips the operator and the polymerase is blocked.
scenes.narration: The three genes are called lacZ, lacY and lacA. One promoter starts all three, and RNA polymerase reads them into a single messenger RNA. Next to them is a fourth gene, lacI. It makes the lac repressor. The repressor binds the operator, a short stretch of DNA at the start of transcription. Bound there, it keeps RNA polymerase from transcribing them.

scenes.tts: Lactose enters the cell through a carrier called the permease. An enzyme, beta-galactosidase, turns a little of it into allolactose. Lactose itself is not the signal. Allolactose is. It binds the repressor and changes its shape. The repressor then holds the operator more weakly, so it comes off, and transcription starts.

scenes.visual: Lactose passes the permease, becomes allolactose, docks on the repressor, its two lobes open and it lifts off the operator; polymerase moves along and a short mRNA grows.
scenes.narration: Lactose enters the cell through a carrier called the permease. An enzyme, β-galactosidase, turns a little of it into allolactose. Lactose itself is not the signal. Allolactose is. It binds the repressor and changes its shape. The repressor then holds the operator more weakly, so it comes off, and transcription starts.

scenes.tts: Lactose alone is not enough. The lac promoter is weak on its own. Full transcription needs an activator called C A P. When C A P is bound to cyclic A M P, it attaches just upstream of the promoter. There it contacts RNA polymerase and helps it bind and start.
scenes.caption: Lactose alone is not enough. The lac promoter is weak on its own. Full transcription needs an activator called CAP. When CAP is bound to cyclic AMP, it attaches just upstream of the promoter. There it contacts RNA polymerase and helps it bind and start.
scenes.visual: CAP with a cyclic AMP badge docks on the CAP site and grips polymerase; the short mRNA becomes long.
scenes.narration: Lactose alone is not enough. The lac promoter is weak on its own. Full transcription needs an activator called CAP. When CAP is bound to cyclic AMP, it attaches just upstream of the promoter. There it contacts RNA polymerase and helps it bind and start.

scenes.tts: Now add glucose. In the classic account, cyclic A M P is higher when glucose is scarce, so C A P is active. When glucose is plentiful, cyclic A M P is lower. Scientists debate how much this matters in living cells. Glucose has a second effect. While glucose is taken up, a transport protein binds the permease and blocks lactose entry. Less lactose in means less allolactose, so more repressor stays on.
scenes.caption: Now add glucose. In the classic account, cyclic AMP is higher when glucose is scarce, so CAP is active. When glucose is plentiful, cyclic AMP is lower. Less lactose in means less allolactose, so more repressor stays on.
scenes.visual: Glucose arrives; cyclic AMP leaves CAP and CAP lets go; a glucose transport protein plugs the permease, lactose and allolactose fade, the repressor returns to the operator.
scenes.narration: Now add glucose. In the classic account, cyclic AMP is higher when glucose is scarce, so CAP is active. When glucose is plentiful, cyclic AMP is lower. Scientists debate how much this matters in living cells. Glucose has a second effect. While glucose is taken up, a transport protein binds the permease and blocks lactose entry. Less lactose in means less allolactose, so more repressor stays on.

scenes.tts: Put the two inputs together. With no lactose, the repressor stays on, and transcription is very low. That holds even when glucose is scarce. With lactose and glucose together, transcription is reduced. Lactose present and glucose scarce gives high transcription. So the rule is simple. The genes switch on only when lactose is present and glucose is scarce.
scenes.visual: A two-by-two grid of lactose against glucose fills in cell by cell: very low, very low, reduced, high.
